Major industrial gas handling companies are active in developing mobile refueling stations; however, their primary focus has been on compressed hydrogen refueling rather than liquid hydrogen (e.g., Plug Power, Air Products, Air Liquide) (Air Liquide 2023; Plug Power 2024; Air Products n.d.). ZeroAvia, a notable aviation fuel cell powertrain developer, is one company working on a liquid hydrogen dispensing mobile refueler. This refueler will be compatible with their ZA2000 aviation powertrain and has been 69 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications. awarded grant funding from the California Energy Commission to engineer the product with minimal hydrogen losses from boil-off (ZeroAvia 2024a). This system is anticipated to dispense LH at 40 kg/min and is projected to have an initial capacity of around 709 kg LH with a goal of 2 2 3,000-kg capacity in the future (ZeroAvia 2024a, 2025). Chart Industries and Absolut Hydrogen are two other companies actively developing LH dispensing infrastructure for applications 2 inclusive of hydrogen-powered flight (Chart Industries 2022; ZeroAvia 2023a). Importantly, companies like ZeroAvia, Chart Industries, and Absolut Hydrogen advancing LH 2 dispensing technology (Chart Industries 2022; ZeroAvia 2023a; Miftakhov 2025) have the ability to gain insights from the existing gaseous hydrogen refueling industry. In California, there are over 60 light- and heavy-duty vehicle hydrogen refueling stations in place with 50 of these stations active in 2025 (California Air Resources Board 2025). Typical gaseous hydrogen dispensing rates at existing stations are around 1 kg/min (Sprik et al. 2017). Over half of the operating hydrogen refueling stations in California were built by True Zero, with many of these stations relying on liquid hydrogen delivery (True Zero, n.d.). Even though hydrogen is dispensed as a gas using a vaporizer, liquid-hydrogen-supplied vehicle refueling stations utilize much of the same infrastructure and procedures as an LH dispensing station would. Namely, 2 LH storage, LH pumps, and LH transfer lines would be largely unchanged and boil-off 2 2 2 mitigation strategies would be similar. A key challenge of first-of-their kind hydrogen refueling stations in California was station reliability (California Air Resources Board 2025). It would be important for LH refueling developers to learn from the mistakes of the first gaseous hydrogen 2 dispensing developers and focus heavily on reliability in their designs so that no aircraft goes without fuel due to dispensing equipment malfunction. Another possible LH refueling method is using exchangeable tanks that could be easily swapped 2 between aircraft flights (Airport Compatibility of Alternative Aviation Fuels Task Force, International Industry Working Group 2025). In this scenario, the modular tanks could be filled outside of the airport premises such that bulk liquid hydrogen storage does not need to take up space at the airport.
